title: Technical Interviews by Field
summary: Prepare for the technical rounds in your field, from coding and valuation questions to case interviews and aptitude tests.

pages.title: Clarify before solving
pages.body: Whatever your field, the first step is the same: make sure you understand the problem. Restate it in your own words, ask about inputs, constraints and the expected output, and confirm any assumptions. Interviewers often leave problems vague on purpose to see whether you ask. Jumping straight into a solution risks solving the wrong problem well.
pages.tip: Say your assumptions out loud: 'I'll assume the data fits in memory — is that fair?'

pages.title: Break it into parts
pages.body: Large problems become manageable when you split them into smaller steps. Outline your plan before diving in: 'First I'll calculate the load, then check it against the limit, then size the component.' This shows structured thinking and lets the interviewer correct your direction early. Start with a simple working approach before optimising or adding complexity.
pages.tip: Write the steps down so both you and the interviewer can follow them.

pages.title: Think out loud
pages.body: Interviewers assess your reasoning, not just the final answer. Narrate what you are doing and why, including options you reject: 'I could use a lookup table here, but a formula is simpler for this range.' If you get stuck, say what you have tried and where you are blocked. Interviewers often give hints to candidates who communicate clearly.
pages.tip: Long silences feel longer to the interviewer; keep narrating even when unsure.

pages.title: Check and reflect
pages.body: When you reach an answer, test it. Try a simple example, an edge case or a quick sense check: does the number have the right units and a plausible size? Then summarise your solution and mention its limitations or how you would improve it with more time. Catching your own mistake impresses interviewers more than never making one.
pages.tip: Always ask yourself, 'Does this answer make sense in the real world?'

quiz.question: What should you do first when given a technical problem?
options: Start calculating immediately
Clarify the problem, constraints and assumptions
Ask for the answer
Explain your previous job
quiz.explanation: Clarifying ensures you solve the right problem, and interviewers often test for it.

quiz.question: Why should you think out loud during a technical question?
options: It fills time until the interview ends
Interviewers only grade the final answer
It lets interviewers assess your reasoning and offer hints
It prevents follow-up questions
quiz.explanation: Your reasoning is what is being assessed, and clear communication invites useful hints.

quiz.question: What is a good final step after reaching an answer?
options: Test it with an example or sense check
Move on without comment
Ask for a harder problem
Rewrite it from scratch
quiz.explanation: Checking with examples and sense checks catches errors and shows rigour.

pages.title: The coding round
pages.body: Most software interviews include live coding on a shared editor or whiteboard. You are judged on problem solving, code quality and communication. Clarify the input and edge cases, describe a brute-force solution, then improve it. Write clean, readable code with meaningful names. When finished, walk through a test case line by line and state the time and space complexity.
pages.tip: Practise on a plain editor without autocomplete; many interview tools lack it.

pages.title: Data structures and algorithms
pages.body: Core topics appear again and again: arrays and strings, hash maps, stacks and queues, linked lists, trees, graphs, sorting and searching, and recursion. Know the typical time complexity of common operations, such as constant-time average lookup in a hash map. Learn to recognise patterns like two pointers, sliding windows and breadth-first search, rather than memorising individual problems.
pages.tip: When you see repeated lookups in a problem, consider whether a hash map helps.

pages.title: System design basics
pages.body: For mid-level and senior roles, expect a system design round: 'Design a URL shortener.' Start with requirements and scale, then sketch the main components — clients, API, services, database, cache. Discuss trade-offs, such as SQL versus NoSQL, or consistency versus availability. There is rarely one right answer; interviewers want to see reasoned choices and awareness of bottlenecks.
pages.tip: Estimate the scale first, such as requests per second and data size.

pages.title: Code review and discussion
pages.body: Some companies show you existing code and ask you to review it. Look for bugs, unclear naming, missing error handling, security issues and missing tests. Give feedback respectfully and explain why a change matters. You may also be asked about your past projects: be ready to explain your design decisions, what went wrong and what you would do differently.
pages.tip: Prepare one project you can explain in depth, including its trade-offs.

quiz.question: After writing your solution in a coding round, what should you do?
options: Submit it immediately without comment
Walk through a test case and state its complexity
Ask the interviewer to test it
Delete it and start a new approach
quiz.explanation: Testing your code and stating complexity shows rigour and understanding.

quiz.question: How should you start a system design question?
options: Choose a database brand
Write code for the API
Clarify requirements and estimate the scale
Draw a detailed class diagram
quiz.explanation: Requirements and scale shape every later design decision.

quiz.question: What should you look for when asked to review code?
options: Only formatting and indentation
The author's name
Whether it uses the newest language version
Bugs, unclear naming, error handling, security issues and tests
quiz.explanation: A good review covers correctness, clarity, robustness, security and testing.

pages.title: The three statements
pages.body: Expect questions on how the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement connect. Net income flows from the income statement to the top of the cash flow statement and into retained earnings on the balance sheet. A classic question: 'Depreciation rises by 10 — walk me through the statements.' Practise this aloud until it becomes automatic.
pages.tip: Always remember the balance sheet must balance at the end of your walk-through.

pages.title: Valuation basics
pages.body: Know the main valuation methods: discounted cash flow, comparable companies and precedent transactions. Be ready to explain enterprise value versus equity value, and why the DCF discounts future free cash flows using a rate such as the weighted average cost of capital. Interviewers care more about your understanding of why each method is used than about memorised formulas.
pages.tip: Be able to explain each method in two sentences to a non-specialist.

pages.title: Excel and modelling tests
pages.body: Many finance roles include a timed Excel test: building a simple model, cleaning data or answering questions from a dataset. Know lookup functions, SUMIFS, pivot tables, absolute and relative references, and basic charting. Keep inputs, calculations and outputs clearly separated and labelled. A tidy, checkable model scores better than a clever one nobody can follow.
pages.tip: Learn keyboard shortcuts for navigation; they save valuable minutes under time pressure.

pages.title: Market awareness
pages.body: You may be asked, 'Tell me about a company or deal you've followed' or 'Where do you think interest rates are heading?' Follow financial news regularly for a few weeks before interviews. Prepare one company and one recent market trend you can discuss with numbers and a clear opinion. It's fine to be uncertain; show your reasoning.
pages.tip: Prepare a short investment pitch: the company, your view, and two supporting reasons.

quiz.question: Where does net income go after the income statement?
options: Only to the balance sheet as cash
To the top of the cash flow statement and into retained earnings
Nowhere else; it stays on the income statement
Directly into enterprise value
quiz.explanation: Net income links all three statements through cash flow and retained earnings.

quiz.question: Which is one of the main valuation methods?
options: Discounted cash flow
Straight-line hiring
Double-entry payroll
Inventory counting
quiz.explanation: DCF, comparable companies and precedent transactions are the core methods.

quiz.question: What makes a model score well in an Excel test?
options: Hiding all formulas
Using as many functions as possible
Clearly separated, labelled inputs, calculations and outputs
Putting everything on one cell
quiz.explanation: A tidy, checkable structure is valued over cleverness.

pages.title: Fundamentals and calculations
pages.body: Mechanical, electrical and civil interviews often test core principles with quick calculations: stress and strain, heat transfer, Ohm's law, power, beam loading or fluid flow. Show your method clearly, write units at every step and state assumptions. Getting the approach right matters more than exact arithmetic. Estimate first, so you can spot an answer that is wildly off.
pages.tip: Review the fundamental formulas of your discipline the week before.

pages.title: Safety first
pages.body: Safety questions are common and serious. You might be asked how you would respond to an unsafe situation on site or what you would do if a design didn't meet safety margins. Show that you would stop work, escalate and follow procedures rather than cut corners under deadline pressure. Mention risk assessment, safety factors and relevant protective measures.
pages.tip: Never suggest compromising safety to meet a schedule, even hypothetically.

pages.title: Standards and codes
pages.body: Engineering work follows codes and standards, such as national building codes, electrical regulations or international ISO standards. You don't need to recite them, but you should explain how you use them: checking designs, documenting compliance and staying up to date. If you mention a standard, be sure you understand what it covers, because follow-up questions are likely.
pages.tip: Name the standards you actually used in a project and explain how.

pages.title: Talking about projects
pages.body: Expect detailed questions about a project from work, internships or university. Explain the problem, your specific role, key design decisions, the tools you used and the results, ideally with numbers. Be honest about what went wrong and what you learned. Bring drawings or a portfolio if appropriate, but check that nothing confidential is included.
pages.tip: Your CV review can help you tighten project descriptions before the interview.

quiz.question: What matters most when solving a calculation in an engineering interview?
options: A clear method with units and stated assumptions
Perfect mental arithmetic without writing
Finishing faster than the interviewer
Using the most advanced formula
quiz.explanation: Method, units and assumptions show sound engineering thinking.

quiz.question: How should you answer a question about an unsafe situation on site?
options: Finish the task quickly and report later
Ignore it if the deadline is close
Stop work, escalate and follow procedures
Ask a colleague to handle it quietly
quiz.explanation: Interviewers look for a clear commitment to safety over deadlines.

quiz.question: What should you be careful about when bringing a portfolio?
options: That it uses colour printing
That nothing confidential is included
That it has more than fifty pages
That it only shows university work
quiz.explanation: Sharing confidential material from past employers is a serious red flag.

pages.title: What a case interview is
pages.body: Consulting and many business roles use case interviews: you get a business problem, such as 'A retailer's profits have fallen — why?', and work through it with the interviewer. They assess structured thinking, comfort with numbers, business sense and communication. Cases are either interviewer-led, where they guide each step, or candidate-led, where you drive the analysis.
pages.tip: Take notes of all numbers and facts given in the prompt.

pages.title: Build a structure
pages.body: After clarifying the objective, take a moment to build a framework that breaks the problem into distinct parts. For falling profits, split into revenue and costs, then break each down further. Adapt frameworks to the case rather than forcing a memorised template. Present your structure clearly before diving in, and ask which area the interviewer would like to explore first.
pages.tip: Ask for thirty seconds to organise your thoughts; it's normal and expected.

pages.title: Estimation and market sizing
pages.body: Market sizing questions ask things like, 'How many coffee cups are sold in a city each day?' Break the problem into logical steps: population, share who drink coffee, cups per person, and so on. State assumptions, use round numbers and calculate step by step. The interviewer cares about your logic; a reasonable approach matters more than the exact figure.
pages.tip: Sanity-check the final number against something you know from daily life.

pages.title: Hypothesis-driven thinking
pages.body: Strong candidates form an early hypothesis and test it: 'I suspect rising costs are the main driver — let me check the cost data.' Update your view as new information arrives. Finish with a clear recommendation: your answer, two or three supporting reasons, risks and next steps. Speak as if presenting to a client's chief executive.
pages.tip: Practise live cases in a mock interview to build speed and structure.

quiz.question: How should you use frameworks in a case interview?
options: Apply one memorised template to every case
Avoid structure to seem creative
Adapt a framework to the specific problem
Let the interviewer build it for you
quiz.explanation: Tailored structures show real thinking; forced templates look mechanical.

quiz.question: In a market sizing question, what matters most?
options: A logical approach with stated assumptions
Knowing the exact official figure
Using precise decimals
Answering in under ten seconds
quiz.explanation: Interviewers assess your logic and assumptions, not the exact number.

quiz.question: How should you end a case interview?
options: By summarising every number you calculated
By asking the interviewer for the answer
By saying more analysis is needed
With a clear recommendation, reasons, risks and next steps
quiz.explanation: A decisive, client-ready recommendation is the expected finish.

pages.title: Take-home assignments
pages.body: Take-home tasks give you hours or days to complete a realistic piece of work, such as a small app, an analysis or a report. Read the brief carefully and deliver exactly what is asked, before adding extras. Respect any suggested time limit. Include a short note explaining your approach, assumptions and what you would improve with more time.
pages.tip: Ask the recruiter how the task will be assessed before you start.

pages.title: Numerical and verbal reasoning
pages.body: Numerical tests use tables and charts to test percentages, ratios and data interpretation. Verbal tests give a passage and ask whether statements are true, false or cannot be determined from the text. For verbal questions, use only the information given, not outside knowledge. Practice tests are widely available and familiarity greatly improves speed and accuracy.
pages.tip: In verbal tests, 'cannot say' is correct when the passage doesn't confirm or contradict the statement.

pages.title: Personality and situational tests
pages.body: Personality questionnaires ask how you typically behave, and situational judgement tests show workplace scenarios with several possible responses. Answer honestly and consistently; many tools detect contradictory answers. Keep the role's requirements in mind, but don't try to invent a different personality. For situational tests, choose responses that are professional, collaborative and address the problem directly.
pages.tip: Read the company values beforehand; situational tests often reflect them.

pages.title: Managing your time
pages.body: Most aptitude tests are strictly timed and designed so that few people finish every question. Check the number of questions and divide the time to set a rough pace. Don't get stuck: skip hard questions and return if time allows. Find out whether wrong answers are penalised; if not, answer every question. Take tests in a quiet place with a stable connection.
pages.tip: Keep a calculator and scrap paper ready if they are allowed.

quiz.question: What should you include with a take-home assignment?
options: A request for a higher salary
A short note on your approach, assumptions and possible improvements
Extra features instead of the requested ones
Nothing beyond the code or file
quiz.explanation: Explaining your reasoning helps reviewers understand and value your work.

quiz.question: In a verbal reasoning test, what information should you use?
options: Your general knowledge on the topic
What seems most likely in real life
Only the information given in the passage
The answer you think the employer prefers
quiz.explanation: Verbal reasoning tests judge statements solely against the passage.

quiz.question: What should you do if you get stuck on a hard question in a timed test?
options: Skip it and return if time allows
Stay on it until you solve it
End the test early
Guess randomly on every remaining question
quiz.explanation: Skipping keeps your pace up so you can answer more questions overall.
